L16: > Abstract:We characterize complex-elliptic operators $\mathbb A(D)$ through a hierarchy of overdeterminacy ($\ell$-vanishing) quantifying the structural twisting of their symbols. This framework yields the optimal dimensional estimate for $BV^{\mathbb A}$-functions: a measure ${\mathbb A} u$ cannot concentrate on sets of dimension below $n-1$. Consequently, the jump part of ${\mathbb A} u$ is characterized as an $(n-1)$-dimensional surface measure with density given by the symbol and the two-sided traces.

L55: # Monotone Sobolev functions:
L56: approximation, critical points, and level sets
L57: 
L58: Deguang Zhong Affiliation: Institute of Applied Mathematics, Shenzhen Polytechnic University, Affiliation: Shenzhen 518055, China Email: huachengzhon@163.com
L59: ###### Abstract
L60: We give an affirmative answer to the planar local smoothing problem in Question 1.7 of D. Ntalampekos and positive and negative answers to the basic approximation and level-set parts of his higher-dimensional Question 1.8.
L61: In every dimension $n\geq 2$, each continuous Lebesgue monotone function in $W^{1,p}$ on a bounded open set admits uniform and strong $W^{1,p}$ approximation by monotone $C^{1,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ functions, with unchanged Sobolev boundary values and no increase of the $p$-Dirichlet energy, for $1<p<\infty$. The energy can be made strictly smaller unless the original function is $p$-harmonic.
L62: In the plane we obtain smooth local replacement at every isolated $p$-harmonic critical point, with arbitrarily small $C^{1}$ and Sobolev error. A point of gradient index $-m$ can be resolved into exactly $m$ nondegenerate saddles. Together with Ntalampekos’s planar theorem, this gives smooth monotone density with fixed boundary values; at a nonsmooth $p$-harmonic minimizer the energy increase is unavoidable but can tend to zero.
L63: In dimensions $n\geq 3$, an explicit Lipschitz monotone function has a nonmanifold point on every level in an interval, although it admits smooth monotone approximation. A product extension of a planar homogeneous $7$-harmonic function also rules out a general discrete exceptional set under the exact boundary and energy constraints. The answer to Question 1.8 thus distinguishes the five basic approximation properties from the stronger topological and exceptional-set conclusions.
L64: Applications include constrained integral functionals, strict $BV$ convergence of superlevel sets, nonlinear flux convergence, and stability of persistence diagrams under tameness assumptions.
L65: Keywords. Lebesgue monotonicity, Sobolev approximation, $p$-harmonic function, double-obstacle problem, quasiregular gradient, critical point, level-set topology.

L68: ## 1 Introduction
L69: ### 1.1 Ntalampekos’s questions and the approximation problem
L70: The principal results of this paper concern two questions posed by D. Ntalampekos [【43†61】, Questions 1.7 and 1.8]. We answer the planar local smoothing problem in Question 1.7 affirmatively. For Question 1.8, we establish the higher-dimensional analogue of the five basic approximation properties, disprove the level-set manifold assertion, and exhibit an obstruction to the additional discrete-exceptional-set conclusion.
L71: These answers form the common purpose of the approximation theorems and the counterexamples below.
L72: The maximum and minimum principles constrain a scalar function without prescribing an equation. Lebesgue introduced this notion of monotonicity in his treatment of the Dirichlet problem [【44†48】]. Ordinary Sobolev smoothing, although available by the Meyers–Serrin theorem [【45†57】], need not preserve both principles. The problem therefore concerns simultaneous control of regularity, boundary values, energy, and the geometry of a scalar field.
L73: ###### Definition 1.1.
L74: 
L75: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold without boundary and without compact connected components. A continuous function $f:M\to\mathbb{R}$ satisfies the maximum principle if
L76: 
L77:  | $$\max_{\overline{V}}f=\max_{\partial V}f\qquad\text{for every nonempty open }V\Subset M.$$  |
L78: It satisfies the minimum principle if $-f$ satisfies the maximum principle. It is monotone in the sense of Lebesgue if it satisfies both, and strictly monotone if neither extremum is attained in the interior of $V$ for any such $V$.
L79: Here $V\Subset M$ means that $\overline{V}$ is compact and contained in $M$. Unless another space is specified, $M$ is an open subset of Euclidean space. Strict monotonicity is equivalent to the absence of local maxima and minima, including nonstrict local extrema: an interior maximizer on $\overline{V}$ is a local maximum, and a local maximum is an interior maximizer on a sufficiently small closed coordinate ball. Thus a $C^{1}$ function with nonvanishing gradient is strictly monotone.
L81: For $1<p<\infty$, we use the standard Sobolev spaces $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ and $W^{1,p}_{0}(\Omega)$; the latter is the closure of $C_{c}^{\infty}(\Omega)$ in the Sobolev norm [【46†17】, 【47†31】]. The condition $v-u\in W^{1,p}_{0}(\Omega)$ specifies unchanged Sobolev boundary values without any regularity assumption on $\partial\Omega$. On a Lipschitz domain it is equivalent to equality of traces. We write
L82: 
L83:  | $$E_{p}(v;D)=\int_{D}|\nabla v|^{p}\,dx,\qquad E_{p}(v)=E_{p}(v;\Omega)$$  |
L84: when the underlying domain is understood. All these energies and Sobolev norms are Euclidean. A subscript $\mathrm{loc}$ denotes local regularity, with no global bound on the corresponding local norms.
L85: Manfredi [【48†54】] developed weak monotonicity through Sobolev truncation principles. Hajłasz and Malý [【49†37】] constructed approximations by locally weakly monotone functions while controlling nonlinear expressions in the gradient. Their starting functions need not be monotone, and the approximants need not be continuous or smooth. Here continuity and scalar monotonicity are retained throughout, and the objective is improved differentiability in a fixed boundary-value class.
L86: Ntalampekos [【43†61】, Theorem 1.4] proved that almost every level of a continuous monotone planar Sobolev function is an embedded one-dimensional topological submanifold with locally finite length. His Theorem 1.6 gives monotone $C^{1,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ approximation with uniform and strong Sobolev convergence, fixed boundary values, and a nonincreasing energy bound.
L87: The approximants are $p$-harmonic on a set of measure arbitrarily close to full and smooth off a discrete set; when $p=2$, they are smooth everywhere. We retain the numbering of the source questions. The first concerns local smoothing in the plane; the second asks for higher-dimensional analogues of the two cited planar theorems.
L88: ###### Question 1.7.
L89: 
L90: For a planar $p$-harmonic function with $1<p<\infty$ and $p\neq 2$, is smooth monotone approximation possible near a critical point, simultaneously in the uniform and $W^{1,p}$ topologies?
L91: This is the planar problem in [【43†61】, Question 1.7]. No nonincreasing-energy condition is imposed there. Our local theorem also keeps the function unchanged outside any prescribed neighborhood and controls the $C^{1}$ error. The case $p=2$, included in our theorem, already has smooth harmonic input.
L92: ###### Question 1.8.
L93: 
L94: Do the level-set and approximation conclusions of [【43†61】, Theorems 1.4 and 1.6] admit higher-dimensional analogues?
L95: Question 【50†1.8】 restates [【43†61】, Question 1.8], which places no separate higher-dimensional restriction on $p$. The cited planar level-set theorem assumes $1\leq p\leq\infty$, whereas the approximation theorem assumes $1<p<\infty$. Our Lipschitz level-set example covers every Sobolev exponent in the former range.
L96: Theorem 【51†A】 gives the affirmative answer for approximation properties (A)–(E), whereas Theorems 【52†E】 and 【53†F】 give the negative answers for the level-set assertion and the general discrete exceptional-set refinement, respectively. Theorem 【54†B】 answers Question 【55†1.7】; Theorems 【56†C】 and 【57†D】 supply its saddle-resolution refinement and global planar consequence.
L97: ### 1.2 Approximation and critical-point replacement
L98: ###### Theorem A.
L99: 
L100: Let $n\geq 2$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}$ be bounded and open, and let $1<p<\infty$. If $u\in C(\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ is monotone, there are $\alpha=\alpha(n,p)\in(0,1)$ and monotone functions $u_{j}\in W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ such that
L101: 
L102:   1. (A)
L103: 
L104: $u_{j}\in C^{1,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ for every $j$;
L105: 
L106:   2. (B)
L107: 
L108: $\sup_{\Omega}|u_{j}-u|\longrightarrow 0$;
L109: 
L110:   3. (C)
L111: 
L112: $u_{j}\longrightarrow u$ strongly in $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$;
L113:

L115: $E_{p}(u_{j};\Omega)\leq E_{p}(u;\Omega)$ for every $j$;
L116: 
L117:   5. (E)
L118:

L120:

Thus Theorem 【51†A】 answers affirmatively the basic approximation part of Ntalampekos’s Question 1.8 in every dimension $n\geq 3$. L191: Level-set topology must be distinguished from level-set measure. Federer’s coarea theory [【95†33】, 【94†34】] and its Sobolev formulation by Malý, Swanson, and Ziemer [【96†52】] control the latter. Alberti, Bianchini, and Crippa [【97†2】] studied Lipschitz level sets and Sard-type properties; Bourgain, Korobkov, and Kristensen [【98†16】] obtained results under Sobolev and bounded-variation assumptions.
L192: Related extensions of Sard’s theorem are due to de Pascale [【99†23】], Bojarski, Hajłasz, and Strzelecki [【100†14】], and Figalli [【101†35】]. These regularity assumptions and conclusions do not turn every finite-measure level of a higher-dimensional Lipschitz monotone function into a hypersurface. Theorem 【52†E】 gives an explicit separation, and Section 【38†12】 shows that it persists even alongside strict $BV$ convergence of superlevel sets.
L193: On metric surfaces, Rajala’s uniformization theorem [【102†63】] uses scalar minimizers and their levels. Ntalampekos’s metric level-set theorem [【43†61】, Theorem 1.5] separates the topological argument from Euclidean differentiation, and his work on Sierpiński carpets [【103†62】] provides another potential-theoretic motivation.
L194: Esmayli and Hajłasz [【104†28】] treated coarea inequalities in metric spaces; Esmayli, Ikonen, and Rajala [【105†29】] established such inequalities for monotone Sobolev functions on metric surfaces. Meier and Ntalampekos [【106†55】] proved a Sobolev coarea inequality and applied it to Lipschitz-volume rigidity. Meier, Vikman, and Wenger [【107†56】] proved monotone Sobolev extension results into metric surfaces with applications to uniformization.

L208: ### 1.4 Answers to Questions 1.7 and 1.8
L209: 
L210: The correspondence between the source questions and our results is summarized below. The distinction between the basic properties (A)–(E) and the additional conclusions is essential to the answer to [【43†61】, Question 1.8].
L211: Question in [【43†61】]  | Result  | Answer and scope
L212: --- | --- | ---
L213: 1.7: planar local smoothing  | Theorem 【54†B】  | Affirmative, with $C^{1}$ control; Theorems 【56†C】 and 【57†D】 give saddle resolution and global smooth density.
L214: 1.8: approximation properties (A)–(E)  | Theorem 【51†A】  | Affirmative for every $n\geq 3$ and $1<p<\infty$, with fixed boundary values and nonincreasing energy.
L215: 1.8: almost-everywhere manifold levels  | Theorem 【52†E】  | Negative for every $n\geq 3$; a Lipschitz example has a nonmanifold point on every level in an interval.

L217: The higher-dimensional $C^{1,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ theorem does not assert that its approximants are $p$-harmonic on an open set of measure arbitrarily close to full. Nor do the counterexamples settle general higher-dimensional $C^{\infty}$ approximation when only convergence of energies, rather than the one-sided bound, is required. The answers to Question 1.8 stated above refer to the precise assertions in the table.

L219: Our applications combine the approximation theorems with established continuity arguments for integral functionals [【111†22】], coarea and perimeter theory [【112†5】], nonlinear error variables [【113†13】, 【114†25】], and persistence stability [【115†21】]. Their common feature is a recovery sequence satisfying the monotonicity and Sobolev boundary constraints, with the appropriate regularity in each dimension.
L905: ## 10 Singular minimizers and higher-dimensional exceptional sets
L906: 
L907: Proposition 【110†2.4】 shows that prescribed Sobolev boundary values and a nonincreasing energy bound fix every $p$-harmonic input. We now make the resulting regularity obstruction explicit. The same homogeneous planar function illustrates both the positive energy cost of planar smoothing and the failure of a discrete exceptional set after extension to higher dimensions.

L96: ###### Remark 1.3.
L97: Our research focuses on proving the existence of infinitely many solutions for superlinear problems under the Ambrosetti-Rabinowitz condition, a direction distinct from the symmetry-breaking perspective. This work settles the long-standing conjecture for the general equation $-\Delta u=f\left(x,u\right)$ under assumptions $\left(f_{1}^{\prime}\right)$-$\left(f_{3}\right)$.
